html:
In 480 BCE Xerxes burned Athens. Seventy-six years later Athens surrendered to Sparta, its walls pulled down. In between it built the Parthenon, invented much of drama and history as we know them, and ran the most radical democracy of the ancient world.

Ships made the democracy

The victory at Salamis was won by rowers, and rowers were poor citizens. Themistocles' fleet gave the poor a reason to claim power, and the democracy grew more radical as the navy grew.

An alliance became an empire

The Delian League began as a free alliance against Persia. Within a generation Athens held its treasury, collected its tribute and crushed members who tried to leave. That money paid the rowers, the jurors and the builders of the Acropolis under Pericles.

The bill came due

Sparta and its allies feared the empire, and the Peloponnesian War began in 431 BCE. The Long Walls made Athens safe from Sparta's army but packed the city just as the plague arrived. The rest of the war, as Thucydides tells it, is a city losing its judgement.

What outlasted it

The empire did not survive, but the thinking did. Socrates was put to death by the restored democracy in 399 BCE; his student Plato answered by founding the Academy, which lasted, in one form or another, for 900 years.
